title: Grade 1 Math Lab
blurb: Sixteen topics. Each one is a short lesson you can see, then puzzles to try.

topics.name: Ten Frames
topics.parentNote: Subitizing. Reading a quantity in one look instead of counting one by one is the foundation of fact fluency.

teach.text: A ten frame is 2 rows of 5. It holds 10.

teach.cap: A full top row is 5. You do not have to count it.

teach.text: So 7 is just a full row and 2 more.

teach.cap: 5 and 2. That is 7.

teach.text: Empty squares matter too. If 7 are full, 3 are empty. 7 and 3 make 10.

exercises.ask: How many?
exercises.why: A full row is 5, and 1 more sits below it. 5 and 1 is 6.

exercises.ask: How many?
exercises.why: 5 on top and 4 below. It is also 1 short of 10, which is the faster way to see it.

exercises.ask: Fill in 8.
exercises.why: Fill the top row of 5 first, then 3 more. That is quicker than counting one at a time.

exercises.ask: How many empty squares?
exercises.why: 7 are full. The frame holds 10. 7 and 3 make 10.

exercises.ask: A ten frame with 4 full has 6 empty.
exercises.why: 4 and 6 make 10. Every ten frame splits into a full part and an empty part that add to 10.

exercises.ask: Two full frames and 4 more. How many?
exercises.why: 10 and 10 is 20. Then 4 more is 24.

exercises.ask: Type a number. We show its partner to 10.
exercises.why: Every pair here adds to 10. Knowing all of them by heart makes bigger addition much easier.

topics.name: Number Bonds
topics.big: Every number is made of smaller parts.
topics.parentNote: Part-whole structure. A single bond gives four facts, which is why fact families are taught together rather than memorised separately.

teach.text: The whole goes on top. The parts go below.

teach.cap: 10 is made of 6 and 4.

teach.text: One bond gives you four facts. All from the same picture.

teach.cap: Learn one bond, get four facts free.

teach.text: If you know the whole and one part, you subtract. If you know both parts, you add.

exercises.ask: What is the missing part?
exercises.why: The whole is 9 and one part is 5. 9 take away 5 is 4.

exercises.ask: What is the whole?
exercises.why: Both parts are known, so you add them. 7 and 3 make 10.

exercises.ask: What is the missing part?
exercises.why: 13 take away 8 is 5. Or count up from 8 to 13, which is 5 steps.

exercises.ask: From the bond 8, 3 and 5 you can write 8 - 5 = 3.
exercises.why: Yes. Take one part off the whole and the other part is left. That is what a bond means.

exercises.ask: Which bond is broken?
exercises.why: 5 and 2 make 7, not 8. The other three all add up correctly.

exercises.ask: Write all four facts for the bond 12, 5 and 7.
exercises.hint: Two adding, two taking away. Then type the whole.

exercises.ask: Type a part of 8. We show the other part.
exercises.why: 8 can be split many ways. Seeing them all is what makes a number feel flexible instead of fixed.

topics.name: Doubles, Odd and Even
topics.big: Even means everyone gets a partner.
topics.parentNote: Parity, taught as pairing rather than as a rule about last digits. An even number IS a doubles fact; an odd number is a double plus one. That link is the real mathematics here.

teach.text: A double is a number added to itself. 4 and 4 is 8.

teach.cap: 8 dots in 2 equal rows. Everyone has a partner.

teach.text: That is what even means. Every one has a partner.

teach.cap: Now 9. The orange dot has nobody. 9 is odd.

teach.text: So every even number is a double. And every odd number is a double plus 1.

exercises.ask: Double 6.
exercises.why: 6 and 6 is 12. Doubles are worth knowing by heart, they make other facts easy.

exercises.ask: Is 7 odd or even?
exercises.why: Pair them up: 3 pairs and 1 left over. One is alone, so 7 is odd.
3 and 3 is 6, and 1 more makes 7. Every odd number is a double plus 1.

exercises.ask: Every double is even.
exercises.why: A double is two equal groups, so everyone has a partner. That is exactly what even means.

exercises.ask: An even number plus an even number is odd.
exercises.why: Two even numbers make an even number. Both groups pair up, so the whole thing pairs up.

exercises.ask: Build 10 as 2 equal rows.
exercises.why: 2 rows of 5. Because it fits into 2 equal rows, 10 is even, and it is the double of 5.

exercises.ask: On paper try 3 + 5, then 7 + 1, then 9 + 3. What is 9 + 3?
exercises.hint: When you have all three answers, look at them together. Odd or even?
exercises.why: 9 + 3 is 12. Now look at all three answers: 8, 8 and 12. Every one is even. Two odd numbers always make an even number, because each odd number has one lonely dot and the two lonely dots pair up with each other.

exercises.ask: Type any even number up to 20.
exercises.why: Even numbers step by 2. They are the numbers you land on when you skip count by twos.

topics.name: The Balance
topics.parentNote: The single highest-value idea on this page. Most children read = as "write the answer", and will call 4 + 5 = 6 + 3 wrong. That misconception is the main obstacle to algebra later.

teach.text: The equals sign is not a button that says "answer here".
It means both sides weigh the same.

teach.cap: Same on both sides. Balanced.

teach.text: So 4 + 5 = 6 + 3 is completely fine. Both sides are 9.
Check both sides on their own. Then see if they match.

exercises.why: Left side is 9. Right side is 9. They match, so it is true. The equals sign is allowed to have sums on both sides.
True. Nothing has to be worked out. Both sides are already the same.
3 and 4 make 7, not 8. The two sides do not match, so the balance tips.
True. The single number is allowed to be on the left. 6 and 4 make 10.
The left side is 7, so the right side must be 7 too. 4 and 3 make 7.
6 and 6 is 12. So the right side must be 12. 10 and 2 make 12.

exercises.ask: 9 + 4 = ? + 5. Work it out on paper.
exercises.why: 9 and 4 is 13. So the right side needs 13. 8 and 5 make 13.

exercises.ask: Type a number. We show what it needs to reach 12.
exercises.why: Every one of these makes a true equation with 12 on the other side.

topics.name: Missing Numbers
topics.big: The mystery number can hide anywhere.
topics.parentNote: MA.1.AR.2.3. Unknowns in the first, second or answer position. Children find the first two positions much harder, so those are practised most here.

teach.text: Usually the missing number is at the end. 3 + 4 = ?
But it can hide at the front. ? + 4 = 7

teach.cap: A bond helps. Whole on top, one part missing.

teach.text: Know the whole and one part, take away. Know both parts, add.

exercises.why: Count up from 7 to 12. That is 5 steps.
11 take away 4 is 7. The missing number is at the front, but it works the same way.
13 down to 8 is 5 steps, so 5 was taken away.
This one is backwards. Something lost 6 and had 7 left, so it started at 13.

exercises.ask: Which one is 9?
exercises.why: 9 and 5 make 14. Choice a is 8, choice c is 8, and choice d is 10.

exercises.ask: Mia had some stickers. She gave away 6 and has 9 left. How many did she start with?
exercises.hint: Draw a bond. The whole is missing.
exercises.why: She gave away 6 and kept 9, so she started with 6 and 9 together, which is 15.

exercises.ask: If ? + 8 = 8, then ? is 0.
exercises.why: True. Adding nothing leaves the number alone. Zero is a real answer.

topics.name: Tens and Ones
topics.big: Big numbers are just bundles of ten.
topics.parentNote: MA.1.NSO.1.2 and 2.3, pushed past 100. Understanding that 10 more changes only the tens digit is what makes mental addition possible later.

teach.text: 47 means 4 tens and 7 ones.

teach.cap: Two full frames is 2 tens, which is 20.

teach.text: Add 10 and only the tens digit moves. 47 becomes 57.

teach.cap: One jump of ten takes 40 to 50.

teach.text: Adding 1 changes the last digit. Adding 10 changes the first one.

exercises.ask: 3 tens and 6 ones is what number?
exercises.why: 3 tens is 30, plus 6 ones, which makes 36.

exercises.ask: 10 more than 47.
exercises.why: Only the tens digit moves. 4 tens becomes 5 tens, and the 7 ones stay.

exercises.ask: 10 less than 62.
exercises.why: 6 tens drops to 5 tens. The 2 ones do not change.

exercises.ask: Which number has 8 tens and 0 ones?
exercises.why: 80 is 8 tens and nothing else. 18 is 1 ten and 8 ones, which is the same digits the other way round.

exercises.ask: 10 more than 95.
exercises.why: This one crosses 100. 9 tens plus 1 ten is 10 tens, which is 100, plus the 5 ones makes 105.

exercises.ask: 63 is bigger than 36.
exercises.why: True. 63 has 6 tens and 36 has only 3 tens. Compare the tens first.

exercises.ask: 58 + 20. Work it out on paper.
exercises.why: 58 to 68 is one ten, 68 to 78 is another. The 8 ones never move.

exercises.ask: Type any number with exactly 4 tens.
exercises.why: Anything from 40 to 49 has 4 tens. Only the ones digit changes.

topics.name: Equal Groups
topics.parentNote: Skip counting turned into arrays. This is the honest start of multiplication, and the commutative property is visible here long before it gets a name.

teach.text: 3 groups of 4 is 4 + 4 + 4.

teach.cap: 3 rows of 4. Twelve dots.

teach.text: You can skip count instead of adding. 4, 8, 12.

teach.cap: Turn it. 4 rows of 3. Still twelve.

teach.text: Turning an array sideways never changes how many dots there are.

exercises.ask: How many dots?
exercises.why: 3 rows of 4. Skip count 4, 8, 12.

exercises.ask: How many dots?
exercises.why: 2 rows of 5, so 5 and 5, which is 10.

exercises.ask: Build 3 rows of 3.
exercises.why: 3, 6, 9. Three equal rows of three make nine.

exercises.ask: Skip count by 5 four times. Where do you land?
exercises.why: 5, 10, 15, 20. That is also 4 groups of 5.

exercises.ask: 3 groups of 4 has the same number as 4 groups of 3.
exercises.why: True, and it is a big deal. It is the same array turned sideways, so it must be the same amount.

exercises.ask: Which one shows 6?
exercises.why: 2 rows of 3 is 6. Choice a is 8, choice c is 9 and choice d is 5.

exercises.ask: 5 bags. Each bag holds 3 apples. How many apples?
exercises.hint: Draw 5 rows of 3, or skip count by 3.
exercises.why: 3, 6, 9, 12, 15. Five groups of three is fifteen.

exercises.ask: 12 dots split into equal rows. Type a number of rows that works.
exercises.why: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 12 all divide 12 evenly. 5 does not, which is why 5 rows always leaves a gap.

topics.name: Patterns and Shapes
topics.big: Find the rule, then keep it going.
topics.parentNote: Growing patterns and shape composition. The triangular-number pattern in exercise 3 is well beyond grade 1 and is deliberately the hardest thing on the page.

teach.text: Some patterns repeat. Some patterns grow.

teach.cap: Growing by 2 each time.

teach.text: To find the rule, ask what changed from one step to the next.
Shapes have patterns too. Two halves make a whole. Four fourths make a whole.

teach.cap: One fourth is shaded. Four equal parts make the whole.

teach.text: If the jump is not the same each time, look at the jumps themselves. They might have their own pattern.

exercises.why: The jump is 2 every time, so 8 and 2 more is 10.
Counting up in threes. 9 and 3 more is 12.
This one shrinks by 2 each step. 16 take away 2 is 14.
The jumps grow: 2, then 3, then 4, then 5. 10 and 5 is 15. These are called triangle numbers.

exercises.ask: Which shape is cut into fourths?
exercises.why: Fourths means four equal parts. Choice a is halves, choice c is thirds, and choice d is not cut at all.

exercises.ask: Two halves make one whole.
exercises.why: True. That is what half means: one of two equal parts.

exercises.ask: 1, 2, 4, 8, ? What is the rule and the next number?
exercises.hint: It is not adding the same number each time.
exercises.why: Each number doubles. 8 doubled is 16. This is a doubling pattern, not a counting one.

exercises.ask: Type any number you land on counting by 5.
exercises.why: Counting by fives lands on numbers ending in 5 or 0, and never anywhere else.

topics.name: Four Colours
topics.big: Colour any map with just four colours.
topics.parentNote: Graph colouring. The statement is simple enough for a six-year-old and it took mathematicians 124 years to prove, finally in 1976 with the first computer-assisted proof in history. Taught successfully to seven-year-olds by the logician Joel David Hamkins.

teach.text: Here is a map. Each country needs a colour.
One rule: countries that share a border cannot match.

teach.cap: Four countries. Every pair touches, so this one needs all four colours.

teach.text: Touching at just a corner does not count. Only a real border.

teach.cap: The two reds only meet at a corner. That is allowed.

teach.text: Nobody has ever drawn a map that needs five. People tried for 124 years.

exercises.ask: Colour this map. No two countries with a border may match.
exercises.why: Two colours are enough here. The two countries of the same colour only touch at a corner, and a corner is not a border.

exercises.ask: Now this one. Try to use only three colours.
exercises.why: Three works. The long country on top borders all three below it, but the left and right ones never touch each other, so they can share.

exercises.ask: This map needs four. Find a way.
exercises.why: Every country here borders every other one, so no two can ever share. Four countries, four colours, and there is no way around it.

exercises.ask: A map has 3 countries and every pair shares a border. How many colours?
exercises.why: Each one touches both others, so no two can match. Three countries all touching means three colours.

exercises.ask: Two countries that meet only at a corner may be the same colour.
exercises.why: True. The rule is about borders, which are lines, not points. A corner is a point.

exercises.ask: Draw your own squiggly map on paper. Colour it with four. How many did you actually need?
exercises.hint: Draw a few loops crossing each other, then colour the pieces. Type 4 when you have finished.
exercises.why: Whatever you drew, four was enough. It always is. That is the theorem, and it took people from 1852 until 1976 to prove it.

exercises.ask: Last one. Four colours, and every country coloured.
exercises.why: Seven countries and still only four colours. That is the surprising part: the map can get as big and messy as you like and four never stops being enough.

topics.name: One Line, No Lifting
topics.big: Some shapes you can draw in one go. Some you cannot.
topics.parentNote: Eulerian paths. The child discovers a rule and then uses it to predict, which is what a theorem is for. This is where graph theory began, with Euler and the bridges of Königsberg in 1736.

teach.text: Draw the whole shape without lifting your pencil. No line twice.

teach.cap: A square. Easy, you can do it.
A square with both crossings. Try it. You cannot.

teach.text: Here is how to tell without trying. Count the lines at each corner.
A corner is odd if an odd number of lines meet there. The orange ones above are odd.
Zero odd corners or exactly two: you can do it. Any other number: nobody can.

exercises.ask: How many lines meet at each corner of a square?
exercises.why: Two lines at every corner. Two is even, so a square has zero odd corners, which means you can draw it in one go.

exercises.ask: A square can be drawn without lifting your pencil.
exercises.why: True. No odd corners at all, so you can even finish back where you started.

exercises.ask: How many odd corners does this have?
exercises.why: The two corners joined by the crossing line have 3 lines each, and 3 is odd. Two odd corners means yes, it can be drawn. Start at one odd corner and you will finish at the other.

exercises.ask: Which one can NOT be drawn in one line?
exercises.why: Choice b has four odd corners, and four is too many. The others have none at all, so they can be drawn and you even end up back at the start.

exercises.ask: A shape with 4 odd corners can be drawn in one line.
exercises.why: False. Only zero or two odd corners will work. Four means it is impossible, and no amount of trying will change that.

exercises.ask: In Königsberg, 4 pieces of land had 3, 3, 5 and 3 bridges. How many odd?
exercises.why: All four are odd numbers, so there are 4 odd corners. That is why nobody could ever walk all seven bridges once. Euler proved it in 1736 and invented a whole branch of mathematics doing it.

exercises.ask: Draw an envelope: a box, a roof, and both crossing lines. One line?
exercises.hint: Count the odd corners first, then try. Start at an odd one. Type 1 for yes, 0 for no.
exercises.why: Yes. The envelope has exactly two odd corners, the two bottom ones. Start at one and you will always finish at the other. It never works if you start anywhere else.

topics.name: The Bees' Secret
topics.parentNote: Tiling and optimisation. The honeycomb conjecture, that hexagons enclose the most area for the least perimeter, was only proved in 1999 by Thomas Hales. The bees had it first.

teach.text: A tiling covers the floor with no gaps and no overlaps.

teach.cap: Squares fit. No gaps.
Regular pentagons do not. Look at the gaps.

teach.text: Triangles work. Squares work. Hexagons work. Pentagons never do.

teach.cap: Hexagons. This is what bees build.

teach.text: A bee eats 8 pounds of honey to make 1 pound of wax. Hexagons save wax, so the shape is worth real food.

exercises.ask: How many sides does a hexagon have?
exercises.why: Six. A honeycomb cell has six sides, and so does every snowflake arm, which is not a coincidence: both are the shape that packs best.

exercises.ask: Which shape leaves gaps?
exercises.why: Pentagons. Five-sided shapes will not sit side by side without leaving gaps, no matter how you turn them. This is why you never see a five-sided honeycomb.

exercises.ask: Triangles can tile a floor with no gaps.
exercises.why: True. Turn every other one upside down and they fit perfectly. Triangles, squares and hexagons are the only regular shapes that do.

exercises.ask: How many hexagons meet at one point in a honeycomb?
exercises.why: Three. Look at any corner in the picture and count. Three hexagons meeting is what makes the walls share, and sharing walls is what saves the wax.

exercises.ask: Bees use hexagons because they hold a lot of honey for very little wax.
exercises.why: True, and it is a real mathematical fact, not just a nice story. It was finally proved in 1999. The bees had been using it for about 100 million years.

exercises.ask: Find something at home made of hexagons or of repeating tiles. Count how many shapes meet at one corner.
exercises.hint: Try a bathroom floor, a football, a chain-link fence, or a picture of a honeycomb. For hexagons the answer is 3.
exercises.why: Hexagons always meet three at a corner. Squares meet four. Triangles meet six. That number is fixed by the shape, and it is why some shapes tile and others cannot.

exercises.ask: Type the number of sides of a shape that tiles with no gaps.
exercises.why: Only 3, 4 and 6 work among the regular shapes. Not 5, not 7, not 8. Just those three, and nobody can add a fourth.

topics.name: Snowflakes and Mirrors
topics.big: Fold it in half. Do the sides match?
topics.parentNote: Symmetry. The idea that runs from a butterfly to a cathedral to particle physics. Zvonkin ran this with preschoolers, session 42, using folded paper and scissors.

teach.text: A mirror line cuts a shape into two halves that match.

teach.cap: Fold a circle anywhere through the middle and it matches. A circle has endless mirror lines.

teach.text: A square has 4 mirror lines. Two straight, two across the corners.

teach.cap: Fold it up and down, side to side, and both ways across the corners.

teach.text: A real snowflake always has 6. Never 5, never 7.
Letters have mirror lines too. A has one. H has two. F has none at all.

exercises.ask: How many mirror lines does a square have?
exercises.why: Four. Up and down, side to side, and the two lines through opposite corners. Try folding a paper square to check.

exercises.ask: How many mirror lines does a triangle with equal sides have?
exercises.why: Three, one from each corner to the middle of the opposite side. A shape with equal sides has one mirror line per side.

exercises.ask: How many arms does a snowflake have?
exercises.why: Six, always. It comes from the way water molecules lock together as they freeze, which happens to make hexagons, the same shape the bees use.

exercises.ask: Which letter has NO mirror line?
exercises.why: F has none. Fold it any way you like and the halves never match. A folds up and down the middle, H folds two ways, and O folds almost any way at all.

exercises.ask: A shape can have more than one mirror line.
exercises.why: True. A square has 4, a hexagon has 6, and a circle has so many you cannot count them.

exercises.ask: Fold paper in half twice, cut the folded edge, open it. How many mirror lines?
exercises.hint: Two folds gives two mirror lines. Try three folds after and see what happens.
exercises.why: Two folds makes two mirror lines. Every fold you add before cutting doubles the matching, which is exactly how paper snowflakes are made.

exercises.ask: Type any number of mirror lines a shape can have.
exercises.why: A shape with equal sides has one mirror line per side, so any of these is possible. Build a shape with 12 sides and it has 12.

topics.name: The Twisted Loop
topics.big: A paper strip with only one side.
topics.parentNote: The Möbius band. The best wow moment in elementary mathematics, and a genuine object topologists still study. Zvonkin used it with five-year-olds, session 21. This topic is mostly scissors and paper on purpose.

teach.text: Cut a long paper strip. Give one end a half twist. Tape the ends together.
Now draw a line down the middle without lifting your pen.
The line comes back to the start, and it has covered the whole strip. Both sides. So it only has one side.
Now cut along that line. It should fall into two loops.
It does not. You get one long loop instead. Try it before you believe it.

exercises.ask: How many sides does a normal paper loop have, with no twist?
exercises.why: Two. The inside and the outside. You cannot get from one to the other without going over the edge.

exercises.ask: How many sides does a loop with one twist have?
exercises.why: One. The twist joins the inside to the outside, so a pen never has to cross the edge. This shape is called a Möbius band.

exercises.ask: Make a normal loop and cut it down the middle. How many loops do you get?
exercises.hint: Paper strip, tape the ends, no twist. Then cut along the middle all the way round.
exercises.why: Two separate loops, exactly as you would expect. Keep this one to compare with the twisted version.

exercises.ask: Now make a twisted loop and cut it down the middle. How many loops?
exercises.hint: Same strip, but give one end a half twist before taping. Cut down the middle.
exercises.why: One. One long loop with a couple of twists in it. It surprises grown-ups too, and there is no trick: it is just what a one-sided surface does.

exercises.ask: The recycling symbol is a twisted loop.
exercises.why: True. Look closely at the three arrows next time. It is a Möbius band, chosen on purpose because it has no end.

exercises.ask: How many edges does a twisted loop have?
exercises.why: One. Run a finger along the rim and you go all the way round and come back without lifting. A normal loop has two rims.

exercises.ask: Cut a twisted loop one third of the way from the edge instead of the middle. How many loops now?
exercises.hint: Keep the same distance from the edge the whole way round. You will go round twice before meeting your start.
exercises.why: Two, but they are linked together and one is twice as long as the other. Nobody would guess that. This is the kind of thing mathematicians spend whole careers on.

topics.name: Socks in the Dark
topics.parentNote: The pigeonhole principle. A genuine proof technique that produces certainty rather than a good guess, and it teaches the difference between 'probably' and 'definitely' which many adults never get straight.

teach.text: A drawer has black socks and white socks all mixed up. The light is broken.
You grab 2 socks. Might they match? Yes. Must they? No.
Grab 3. Now there are only 2 colours, so 2 of your 3 have to be the same.

teach.cap: Three socks, two colours. Two of them must match.

teach.text: 10 socks or 10,000 makes no difference. Three is always enough. That is what makes it maths, not luck.

exercises.ask: 2 sock colours in the drawer. How many must you grab to be SURE of a pair?
exercises.why: Three. With only 2 colours, the third sock has to match one of the first two. There is nowhere else for it to go.

exercises.ask: Grabbing 2 socks might give you a pair.
exercises.why: True, it might. But might is not the same as must, and this topic is about must.

exercises.ask: 3 sock colours now. How many to be sure of a pair?
exercises.why: Four. Three could all be different, one of each colour. The fourth has no new colour left to be.

exercises.ask: 5 sock colours. How many to be sure?
exercises.why: Six. Always one more than the number of colours. That is the whole rule, and it never changes.

exercises.ask: A drawer with 1000 black and 1000 white socks needs more than 3 grabs.
exercises.why: False, and this is the surprising part. How many socks are in there makes no difference at all. Only the number of colours matters.

exercises.ask: In a room of 13 people, how many must share a birth month?
exercises.why: Two. There are only 12 months, so with 13 people two of them must land in the same one. You do not need to know a single thing about any of them.

exercises.ask: There are 8 socks in the drawer: 4 red, 4 blue. You want 2 BLUE ones for certain. How many must you grab?
exercises.hint: Think about the worst possible luck. What if you pull out every red one first?
exercises.why: Six. The worst case is all 4 red first, then 2 blue. Asking for a matching pair is easy. Asking for a particular colour means planning for the worst luck there is.

topics.name: The Tower
topics.big: Move the stack. Never a big disc on a small one.
topics.parentNote: Tower of Hanoi. Recursion and doubling. The child finds 1, 3, 7, 15, 31 themselves, which is double-and-add-one. Zvonkin used it in session 23.

teach.text: Three pegs. A stack of discs, biggest at the bottom.
Move the whole stack to another peg. One disc at a time.
One rule: a bigger disc may never sit on a smaller one.

teach.cap: Look at the moves. What is happening each time?

teach.text: Double the last one and add 1. So 5 discs takes 31, and 6 takes 63.

exercises.ask: 1 disc takes 1 move. How many for 2 discs?
exercises.why: Three. Small one off, big one across, small one back on top. There is no shorter way.

exercises.ask: How many moves for 3 discs?
exercises.why: Seven. Move the top two across, which takes 3, move the big one, which takes 1, then move the two back, another 3. So 3 and 1 and 3.

exercises.ask: 4 discs?
exercises.why: Fifteen. Double 7 and add 1. The pattern is 1, 3, 7, 15, and every step doubles and adds one.

exercises.ask: 5 discs?
exercises.why: Thirty-one. Double 15 is 30, plus 1. You can now work out any number of discs without moving a single one.

exercises.ask: Each extra disc roughly doubles the work.
exercises.why: True, and doubling gets out of hand fast. Ten discs is over a thousand moves. Twenty discs is over a million.

exercises.ask: Use 3 coins of different sizes and 3 spots on the table. Move the stack. How many moves did you use?
exercises.hint: Big coin at the bottom. Never put a bigger coin on a smaller one. Seven is the best possible.
exercises.why: Seven if you did it perfectly. More than that means there was a wasted move somewhere. Try again and see if you can hit exactly 7.

exercises.ask: 6 discs?
exercises.why: Sixty-three. There is an old story about monks moving 64 discs, and the world ending when they finish. At one move a second that would take longer than the universe has existed, so there is no rush.

topics.name: Handshakes
topics.big: Three puzzles that are secretly the same one.
topics.parentNote: Combinatorics and isomorphism. Recognising that two different-looking problems are the same problem is close to a definition of mathematical maturity. Zvonkin spent several sessions on exactly this, sessions 45 to 47.

teach.text: Everyone at a party shakes hands once with everyone else.

teach.cap: 4 people. Each dot is a person, each line a handshake. Count them: 6.

teach.text: Now a different puzzle. 4 dots on paper. Join every pair with a line. How many lines?
Also 6. It is the same picture. It was the same puzzle all along.
1, 3, 6, 10, 15. The same numbers as the triangle pattern. Three puzzles, one answer.

exercises.ask: 2 people shake hands. How many handshakes?
exercises.why: Just one. They shake with each other, and that is the whole party.

exercises.ask: 3 people?
exercises.why: Three. Call them A, B and C. AB, AC, BC. Nobody shakes their own hand and nobody shakes twice.

exercises.ask: 4 people?
exercises.why: Six. Count the lines in the picture. The new person shakes with all 3 who were already there, so 3 more than last time.

exercises.ask: 5 people?
exercises.why: Ten. The fifth person adds 4 handshakes to the 6 you already had. Each new guest shakes with everyone already in the room.

exercises.ask: Joining every pair of 5 dots needs the same number of lines as 5 people shaking hands.
exercises.why: True. They are the same puzzle wearing different clothes. Spotting that is one of the most useful things a mathematician does.

exercises.ask: Draw 6 dots on paper. Join every pair. Count the lines.
exercises.hint: Go dot by dot. The first joins to 5, the next to 4 new ones, then 3, then 2, then 1.
exercises.why: Fifteen. And 5 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 is 15, which is why these are called triangle numbers: stack those rows up and you get a triangle.

exercises.ask: Type a handshake number: 2 people, 3 people, 4 people, and so on.
exercises.why: 1, 3, 6, 10, 15, 21, 28. The gaps between them grow by one each time, because each new guest adds one more handshake than the last one did.

tracks.name: Big ideas
tracks.blurb: Real mathematics. Maps, bridges, bees and a paper loop with one side. This is the kind that makes people want to be mathematicians.

tracks.name: Number skills
tracks.blurb: Getting quick and sure with numbers. Useful, and it makes the big ideas easier to reach.
